titre: Sugar and Hyperactivity: What Mothers Saw in a Placebo
accroche: Twenty-three double-blind studies find no effect of sugar on children's behavior. Another shows what parents believe they see.
contenu_vulgarise:
A birthday party, children running in every direction, and an explanation everyone shares: it's the cake. The idea that sugar makes children hyperactive seems to come from direct observation. Yet it has been tested several times with protocols in which neither the child, nor the parent, nor the observer knows what was consumed.

## What Double-Blind Trials Show

In 1994, Wolraich and his colleagues follow 48 children: 25 of preschool age and 23 of school age, the latter chosen because their parents describe them as sensitive to sugar. Each family follows three diets of three weeks each: one high in sucrose, the other two low in sucrose and sweetened with aspartame or saccharin. The sucrose doses exceed the ordinary, about 5,600 milligrams per kilogram per day in the youngest. In the school-age children judged sensitive, none of the 39 behavior and cognition variables differs from one diet to another. In the preschoolers, 4 measures out of 31 differ, with no consistent pattern.

In 1995, Wolraich, Wilson, and White gather the comparable studies: 16 reports, or 23 studies in which each child receives, in turn, sugar and a sweetened placebo, without anyone knowing which. For each of the 14 behavior or cognition measures, the 95% confidence interval of the mean effect contains zero. The authors conclude that sugar affects neither children's behavior nor their cognitive performance. They specify that a small effect, or an effect on certain subgroups, cannot be ruled out.

## The Experiment Where the Placebo Is Enough

It remains to explain why so many parents are sure of what they observe. Also in 1994, Hoover and Milich recruit 35 boys aged 5 to 7 whom their mothers judge sensitive to sugar. The mothers are randomly divided into two groups. Some are told that their son has just received a large dose of sugar, the others that he received a placebo. In reality, all the boys received aspartame.

The mothers in the first group judge their son markedly more hyperactive. The video recordings reveal something else: they stay closer to him, exert more control, and tend to criticize him, look at him, and talk to him more. The sugar did not change the child. The belief changed the mother, and it is the mother whom the experiment measures.

## The Shift

The hyperactivity attributed to sugar is therefore, at least in part, in the way the child is looked at: the same scene, with the same sweetener, is read as more agitated as soon as the mother believes in sugar. The authors of the 1995 meta-analysis invoke parents' expectations and common associations. The association is real; the cause pointed to is not.

This work says nothing about teeth, the scale, or diabetes, which it does not measure. It says only that what many parents see is not what sugar does to behavior. What remains is what the trials cannot rule out: a small effect, in a subgroup of children that no one has yet isolated.

repere.texte: Meta-analysis of 16 reports (23 double-blind studies, children receiving sugar and a sweetened placebo in turn): for the 14 behavior and cognition measures, the 95% confidence interval of the mean effect contains zero. Mean effect sizes range from -0.14 (direct observations) to +0.30 (school tests).
repere.source: Abstract of Wolraich, Wilson & White, “The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children. A meta-analysis,” JAMA, 1995, vol. 274, no. 20, pp. 1617-1621

carte.punch: Mothers see more hyperactivity in their son after “sugar.” It was aspartame.
carte.idee: In 1994, 35 boys all receive aspartame, but half the mothers are told it is sugar. These mothers judge their son more hyperactive. A meta-analysis of 23 double-blind studies (1995) finds no effect of sugar on behavior.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Wolraich et al., NEJM 1994: PubMed record of the trial on 48 children
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full protocol: three successive diets, same families, weekly assessment.

quiz.question: In the Hoover and Milich experiment (1994), why do the mothers in the first group judge their son more hyperactive?
choix: Because their sons had actually received a large dose of sugar
Because they had been told their son had received sugar, when he had received aspartame
Because aspartame itself makes children more agitated than sugar does
Because the mothers in the control group had been misinformed about the product
quiz.explication: All the boys had received aspartame: only the information given to the mothers changed. They judged their son more hyperactive and controlled him more, which shows the weight of expectation. Sugar does not explain the result, and nothing indicates that aspartame is stimulating: Wolraich's trials found no effect of either sugar or aspartame.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the Wolraich et al. trial (1994), what does the comparison of the three diets show in the school-age children judged sensitive to sugar?
choix: That 4 of the 31 measures differ depending on the diet followed
That none of the 39 behavior and cognition variables differs from one diet to another
That the sucrose doses far exceeded nutritional needs
That only preschool children react to sugar, never the older ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the school-age children judged sensitive, the three diets (high in sucrose, aspartame, saccharin) produce no difference on the 39 variables measured. The differences observed, 4 measures out of 31 with no consistent pattern, concern the preschoolers, not the school-age children.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the meta-analysis by Wolraich, Wilson, and White (1995), what does the 95% confidence interval of the mean effect of sugar show, for each of the 14 measures studied?
choix: That it systematically excludes the value zero, confirming a real effect
That it covers only studies conducted single-blind
That it contains zero for each of the 14 behavior or cognition measures
That it varies too much from one study to another to be calculated
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For each of the 14 behavior or cognition measures, across the 23 double-blind studies, the 95% confidence interval of the mean effect contains zero, which does not allow concluding that sugar has an effect. Nothing indicates a systematic effect, or a calculation problem.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does this work on sugar and behavior not measure?
choix: The effects of sugar on teeth, weight, and diabetes
Children's behavior during the three weeks of diet
The scores obtained on school tests during the trial
The frequency of agitation episodes observed directly
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The trials cited measure behavior and cognitive performance, including scores on school tests and direct observations of agitation, but not the effects of sugar on oral health, weight, or diabetes risk, which they do not measure.
